020.subtitle: The portrait reaches the feet, and beauty is named at its source

commentary.meaning: With this verse the long portrait that began several ślokas ago reaches the ground. The description has come down from her crown through her face, her throat, her arms, her waist and her thighs, and the forty-sixth name finally arrives at the feet — the last limb in the sequence, and in devotional terms the first, since the feet are what a worshipper actually approaches. The name is enormous, twenty-two syllables filling an entire half-verse, and it is built so that the ear reaches the feet only after passing through the sound of the anklets that announce them. Then the portrait, having finished, sets the figure in motion: she walks, and the walk is unhurried. The verse closes by refusing to itemise anything further. Rather than name one more beautiful part, it calls her the hoard out of which beauty is issued — a move from description to source that clears the way for the hymn to leave the body behind in what follows.
commentary.history:
The long stretch of the sahasranāma that precedes this verse is a keśādi-pādānta varṇana, a description running from the hair down to the feet, and this is where it ends. The convention is old and pervasive in Sanskrit devotional poetry: the deity is contemplated limb by limb in a fixed downward order, so that the mind is given somewhere definite to go and cannot wander off. What the order accomplishes at the end is a kind of arrival. The meditation begins where the worshipper cannot reach and finishes where he can, at the feet, which is also where his head goes when he prostrates. In Śrīvidyā the point is made explicit by the pādukā, the sandal: the initiate receives a pādukā-mantra naming the feet of the teacher, and ritual sequences are begun by invoking it. Feet in this tradition are not a modest afterthought to a portrait; they are the joint at which the divine and the human are in actual contact.

Mañjīra is one of several Sanskrit words for the anklet — nūpura is the commonest — and it names specifically the hollow ornament with beads or pellets inside that sounds as the wearer moves. Śiñjāna is the present participle of the root śiñj, to jingle or tinkle, a verb that exists almost entirely to describe this sound and the twang of a bowstring. Editions and manuscripts differ over whether the name opens with the palatal sibilant, śiñjāna, or the dental, siñjāna; the two spellings are both current, and this repository's own text of the verse line and its text of the name happen to disagree, which is a fair sample of the state of the tradition. Nothing doctrinal turns on it, but a reciter following one printed text alongside a chanter following another will notice at once. Poetically the anklet does something no other ornament does: it makes the wearer audible before she is visible. Sanskrit poets use the detail constantly for a woman's approach in darkness, and the devotional application follows without strain — she is heard first. Commentators who read the hymn through the vocabulary of subtle sound take the tinkling as an image of nāda, the unstruck resonance at the base of speech; others take it as jewellery on a body, and the verse supports both.

Marālī is the feminine of marāla, a word used both for the swan and for the flamingo and effectively interchangeable in poetry with haṃsa. Comparing a woman's walk to a swan's is one of the fixed similes of the literature, standing alongside the comparison to an elephant's gait; what the two have in common is deliberateness, weight carried without visible effort, a refusal to hurry. But the swan brings a heavier load of meaning with it. In the Upaniṣadic and later literature the haṃsa is the emblem of discrimination, on the strength of the belief that it can drink the milk out of a mixture of milk and water and leave the water behind — which is why paramahaṃsa became the title of the renunciate who has separated the real from the apparent. The syllables of the word are also read as the breath itself, and reversed they give so'ham, "I am that." A name that says she moves like a swan is therefore saying something, for a reader inside the tradition, about the rhythm of breathing as well as about a queen crossing a floor.

Lāvaṇya, the operative word in the last name, is built from lavaṇa, salt, and means literally saltiness or savour. Sanskrit aesthetics distinguishes it sharply from rūpa, which is form or shape: the handbooks define lāvaṇya as the shimmer that appears within well-made limbs the way light appears to move inside a pearl — not the proportions themselves but the lustre that inhabits them. It is the part of beauty that cannot be specified, and calling her its treasury rather than its possessor is a strong claim, since it makes every individual beautiful thing a withdrawal from a store that is hers. Śevadhi is an old word, at home in Vedic and epic Sanskrit, for a hoard of buried treasure — what a king keeps rather than what he spends. It is grammatically masculine and it stays masculine here even though it describes the goddess, which is why the nāmāvalī form is mahālāvaṇyaśevadhaye rather than the -āyai the neighbouring names take.
commentary.practice:
The first name occupies the entire opening line and is among the longest in the stotra. Attempted whole, it defeats most beginners; the way through is to learn it as four pieces that are individually easy — śiñjāna, maṇimañjīra, maṇḍita, śrīpadāmbujā, that is tinkling, jewelled-anklet, adorned, blessed-lotus-feet. Secure each one separately, then run them together with no gap at all, since the whole thing is a single word and a breath inside it is an error.

The line is a drill in nasals, and that is not accidental; it is what makes it sound like jingling. The palatal ñ appears twice, in ñjā and ñjī, the retroflex ṇ three times, the dental n once, the labial m repeatedly. The palatal cluster ñj is what English speakers get wrong. It is near the middle of "banjo", but the tongue must lie flat against the hard palate for both consonants rather than touching the ridge behind the teeth. The retroflex ṇḍ of maṇḍita wants the tongue tip curled back to the roof of the mouth for both sounds. If the ṇ of maṇi and maṇḍita comes out as an English n, the line loses the alternation of dark and bright nasals on which its effect depends.

Śrī in śrīpadāmbujā is one syllable and not two: palatal ś, then r, then long ī, with nothing inserted between the consonants. The half-verse ends on °ambujā with a long final vowel, and the caesura falls there, after the sixteenth syllable, where the anuṣṭubh always breaks.

In marālīmandagamanā the long vowels of marālī should be given their full value, and the nd of manda is a dental cluster — both consonants made at the teeth — which must not slide back toward the retroflex ṇḍ practised in the line above. Mahālāvaṇyaśevadhiḥ brings the retroflex nasal back, this time before a palatal glide: ṇy is one joined articulation, the curled tongue releasing directly into y. The closing visarga is a light breath coloured by the vowel before it, so dhiḥ ends with a faint echo of hi rather than a hard h.

For the recitation done as archanā, with namaḥ appended to each name, this verse contains a useful irregularity. The first two names take the ordinary feminine dative in -āyai: śiñjānamaṇimañjīramaṇḍitaśrīpadāmbujāyai namaḥ, marālīmandagamanāyai namaḥ. The third does not, because śevadhi is a masculine i-stem and keeps its own declension, giving mahālāvaṇyaśevadhaye namaḥ. Reciters who have settled into the rhythm of -āyai routinely get this one wrong, and it is worth marking in the text.

What the verse asks of the person chanting it is slowness, and it says so twice — once in the name that describes her gait, and once in the construction of the first line, which cannot be hurried without collapsing into a blur of nasals. The portrait has been descending for several verses and it now touches the ground. It is customary to let the attention rest at the feet here rather than move on at once, both because the feet are the part of the image a worshipper is entitled to touch and because the hymn is about to leave the body altogether.

crossReferences.deva: पदन्यासक्रीडापरिचयमिवारब्धुमनसः स्खलन्तस्ते खेलं भवनकलहंसा न जहति । अतस्तेषां शिक्षां सुभगमणिमञ्जीररणितच्छलादाचक्षाणं चरणकमलं चारुचरिते ॥
crossReferences.iast: padanyāsakrīḍāparicayam ivārabdhumanasaḥ skhalantas te khelaṃ bhavanakalahaṃsā na jahati | atas teṣāṃ śikṣāṃ subhagamaṇimañjīraraṇitacchalād ācakṣāṇaṃ caraṇakamalaṃ cārucarite ||
crossReferences.translation: The swans of your palace, as though they had set their minds on learning the play of your footfall, stumble at it and still will not give up the game. And so, lady of lovely ways, your lotus foot goes on giving them their lesson, under cover of the ringing of its beautiful jewelled anklet.
crossReferences.relevance: The same two images the sahasranāma sets side by side — maṇimañjīra and the gait of the swan — worked into a single conceit. The poem reverses the direction of the comparison: it is not that she walks like a swan, but that the swans are trying, badly, to walk like her, and the anklet is the sound of the instruction. Reading it beside the verse is the quickest way to see that these are not two independent ornaments of speech but one long-running poetic association.

crossReferences.deva: तनीयांसं पांसुं तव चरणपङ्केरुहभवं विरिञ्चिः सञ्चिन्वन् विरचयति लोकानविकलम् । वहत्येनं शौरिः कथमपि सहस्रेण शिरसां हरः सङ्क्षुद्यैनं भजति भसितोद्धूलनविधिम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: tanīyāṃsaṃ pāṃsuṃ tava caraṇapaṅkeruhabhavaṃ viriñciḥ sañcinvan viracayati lokān avikalam | vahaty enaṃ śauriḥ katham api sahasreṇa śirasāṃ haraḥ saṅkṣudyainaṃ bhajati bhasitoddhūlanavidhim ||
crossReferences.translation: Gathering the least particle of dust that comes from the lotus of your foot, the creator fashions the worlds entire. The lord of the Yādavas bears that same particle, and barely manages it, on a thousand heads. Hara grinds it fine and uses it for the rite of smearing himself with ash.
crossReferences.relevance: Why a hymn spends its longest single name on a pair of feet. The three great gods are each given a task, and each task is defined by what he can do with the dust from her feet; the whole cosmology is scaled against that one detail. It sets the value the tradition places on śrīpadāmbuja before the sahasranāma's compound is unpacked.

references.title: The Saundaryalaharī, or Flood of Beauty
references.author: ed. and tr. W. Norman Brown (Harvard Oriental Series 43, Harvard University Press, 1958)
references.note: The scholarly edition in English, with the Sanskrit, a literal translation and notes that take the ritual apparatus seriously instead of aestheticising it. Verses 2 and 91, both quoted above, are the closest thing in the literature to a poetic commentary on this verse of the sahasranāma.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma, with the Saubhāgyabhāskara of Bhāskararāya
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library / Theosophical Publishing House)
references.note: The commentary that the whole later tradition argues with. Its treatment of the physical description is worth reading in bulk rather than name by name, because Bhāskararāya's habit is to give several readings of a name and let them stand together, which tells you more about how the hymn was actually used than any single interpretation would.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Sir Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Worth opening for three words in this verse specifically. Look up lāvaṇya and follow it back to lavaṇa, salt; look up śevadhi and notice how old and how concrete it is; look up śiñj and see how narrow the range of the root is. The entries make the verse's imagery legible in a way no translation does.

references.title: An Anthology of Sanskrit Court Poetry: Vidyākara's Subhāṣitaratnakośa
references.author: tr. Daniel H. H. Ingalls (Harvard Oriental Series 44, Harvard University Press, 1965)
references.note: Not a devotional book at all, which is the point. Ingalls's introduction and the sections on women and on the seasons show the conventions this verse is drawing on — the swan's gait, the sounding anklet, the vocabulary of lāvaṇya — in their secular habitat, and the hymn reads very differently once you can hear that it is speaking the ordinary poetic language of its time.

references.title: Śrī Lalitā Sahasranāma Stotram
references.author: M. S. Subbulakshmi (HMV / Saregama)
references.note: The recording by which most people in South India know the text, and useful here because of how she handles the long compound: the nasals stay distinct at speed, which is exactly the thing a learner needs to hear done correctly before attempting it.
